links.note: A compass beside a bar magnet reads wrong because its needle is itself a magnet and is deflected - Activity 4.6's finding in 32692. 32689 describes correct use; this item is about the interference.
The leading statement is the single-pole trap, and 32687 is where the chapter rules it out - poles always exist in pairs, even in the smallest piece.
The N-N, N-S, S-N, S-S table is the attraction/repulsion rule of 32691, established in Activity 4.5.
Re-pushing the suspended magnet to see whether it rests on the same line is Activity 4.3 verbatim - 32688.
The answer is the stroking method of Activity 4.4 - one pole, one direction, repeated - applied to a screwdriver. 32690 is where that method is taught; 32697 only poses the puzzle.
Lodestone as the naturally occurring magnet - 32684, which also gives the natural/artificial distinction.
Magnetic materials defined by being attracted to a magnet, with iron, nickel and cobalt named - 32686.
Non-magnetic materials defined in 32686, the pair of definitions drawn from Table 4.1.
The poles as the ends where the iron filings crowd - Activity 4.2 in 32687.
Breaking a magnet still leaves both poles in every piece - stated in 32687.
A freely suspended magnet resting north-south - Activity 4.3's result in 32688, explained by the Earth behaving as a giant magnet.
The magnetic compass and its freely rotating needle - 32689, which describes the box, pin and dial.
An older floating form of the same instrument: the item asks how a magnetic compass is built, which is 32689's subject. The matsya-yantra itself is not in the concept text.
Reshma's storm with no visible stars, answered by the magnetic compass, is 32683's opening problem verbatim; 32689 explains how the device works rather than naming it in the story.
Wood among non-magnetic materials against the three magnetic metals - 32686's two groups.
An iron bar is attracted by both poles, so only repulsion identifies a magnet - the conclusion 32691 draws from repeating Activity 4.5 with an iron bar.

What Reshma found out for her story - that travellers used a magnetic compass - 32683.
